slides.texte_overlay:
How to master the art of
telling a good story
Start in the middle of the action. Not "So, last Tuesday I woke up..." but "I was standing in the rain with no keys." Jumping straight in grabs attention from the first line.
Cut the details nobody needs. The exact day, the street name, who else was there. If it doesn't make the story funnier or more tense, drop it. Shorter is almost always better.
Build to one moment. Every good story has one turning point, the surprise or the punchline. Slow down right before it, pause, then deliver it. Timing does half of the work.
Use real dialogue. "And he looks at me and says, 'You're in the wrong wedding.'" Quoting people makes a story feel alive and lets your listener picture the scene instantly.
Try this for 30 days: five minutes a day of history, art or science. History is full of incredible stories, and you'll always have a great one ready to tell.
slides.texte_sophia: Try this for 30 days: five minutes a day on a micro-learning app like the Sophia app. History, art, science. History is full of incredible stories, and you'll always have one ready.

slides.texte_overlay: Laugh at yourself in your stories. The best stories are rarely about how great you are. Showing your mistakes makes people relax, laugh and like you a lot more.
Read the room and keep it short. Watch your listeners. If eyes wander, get to the point. A two-minute story told well beats a ten-minute one that everyone politely survives.
